newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian killer pleads "enzyme defence" in appeal.
newsitem.headline: Italian killer pleads "enzyme defence" in appeal.

text.p: Lawyers for a convicted murderer asked an Italian appeal court on Thursday to review the case, arguing that an enzyme imbalance could prove their client had been temporarily deranged when he killed his ex-lover.

In what they claimed as a legal and forensic first in Italy, the lawyers told the court in Milan that new scientific evidence showed that abnormally high levels of the enzyme creatine kinase (CPK) in a person's blood were a pointer to mental illness.

One of the lawyers, Guglielmo Gulotta, said the court should allow a biological psychiatrist to examine Angelo Ortolina, a 41-year-old primary school teacher sentenced to 17 years in jail for premeditated murder.
"They will decide tomorrow," Gulotta said in a telephone interview.
CPK is an enzyme found in some muscular tissue including the heart.

Gulotta said the high CPK levels in Ortolina's blood at the time he shot his former mistress Maria Antonia Magni in May 1995 showed he had been suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder and was therefore incapable of knowing right from wrong.
"We think he should be acquitted," Gulotta said.
Italian newspapers on Thursday portrayed CPK as a "killer enzyme" but Gulotta, who is a professor of forensic psychology, said he had been misquoted and that the idea was "rubbish".
"It is a biological marker," he said.

"A biological tracer such as CPK can signal a transitory psychiatric illness," Gulotta said. He said Ortolina's illness had been brought on by stress caused by pressure from Magni when his client told her he wanted to end their affair.
Ortolina's CPK levels were measured during tests he was having just before the shooting but were not cited as evidence at his trial. The levels returned to normal after the killing.
Gulotta said he had discovered the link between CPK and mental illness through research on the Internet and Medline, a medical database, since no studies had been conducted in Italy.
La Repubblica quoted a scientist unconnected with the case as saying the defence broke new ground in forensic psychiatry though he did not believe the enzyme triggered violence.
"Creatine kinase is released by the organism each time there is very intense muscular activity," psychiatrist Enrico Smeraldi told the newspaper.
"It is present in great quantities in the organism of athletes who have undergone particularly tiring training but that does not mean they become dangerously aggressive," he said.
